primary_secondary.note: Own interviews plus own ML datasets and classifiers.

study_type.claude: Mixed methods (multi-method: qualitative interviews + applied ML research)
study_type.nlm: Mixed methods (qualitative interviews + applied ML research using CRISP-DM)

research_method.claude: Multi-method: semi-structured online interviews with software managers (thematic analysis, follow-up inquiries); applied ML research with CRISP-DM: transfer learning with four pre-trained CNNs for screenshots, grid search over SVC and six other TF-IDF classifiers for URL+text content; Figma design concept of a web application
research_method.nlm: Mixed methods: semi-structured interviews (thematic analysis) + applied ML research using CRISP-DM; EfficientNetV2B0, VGG16, InceptionV3, ResNet50V2 for screenshots; SVC best of 7 classifiers with GridSearchCV for URL text; Figma web application concept
research_method.value: Multi-method (mixed): semi-structured online interviews with 12 software managers, thematic analysis and follow-up inquiry; applied ML research following CRISP-DM: transfer learning with four pre-trained CNNs (EfficientNetV2B0, InceptionV3, ResNet50V2, VGG16) for screenshot classification and seven TF-IDF text classifiers with grid search (best SVC) for URL content; Figma design concept of a monitoring web application
research_method.note: The web application is a design concept only; no productivity outcome is validated.

context.claude: industry; 6 private Indonesian software houses (Batam, Medan, Jakarta; ERP, industrial automation, delivery platforms), 12 managers; ML data from one cooperating software house (2,210 screenshots, 849 URLs) plus Kaggle URL dataset; 2,190 images and 3,563 text records after cleaning
context.nlm: industry; 6 private software companies in Indonesia (Batam, Medan, Jakarta; ERP, industrial automation, delivery platforms), 12 managers; 2,190 screenshots and 3,563 text/URL entries (partner company + Kaggle)
context.value: industry; six privately owned software houses in Indonesia (mainly Batam, Medan, Jakarta; ERP, industrial automation, delivery platforms), 12 software managers interviewed; ML datasets from one cooperating software house plus a Kaggle URL dataset (2,190 screenshots and 3,563 text records after cleaning)
context.note: Number of monitored developers not reported.

ai_discussed.note: ML classifiers (CNN transfer learning, SVC) are the proposed instrument for measuring developer activity; Copilot studies also cited.

remote_covid.note: Interviews were held online; developers' work mode not reported by either.

data_window.note: Only Claude states a period (interviews March–July 2024; ML data July–September 2024); NotebookLM gives none.

cat_productivity.note: On-time task completion, story points completed, and proportion of work-related entries as productivity estimate.

cat_quality.note: Weak: code quality appears only in managers' definitions and reported measurement practice (interviews).

cat_collaboration.note: Monthly peer feedback meetings and anonymous internal peer-assessment survey reported by managers.

cat_satisfaction.note: Borderline: only 'client feedback' as a manager indicator (Claude) and burnout/well-being as factor or future work; no developer satisfaction metric.

cat_activity.note: Git code-contribution tracking and real-time activity monitoring reported; effective working time from activity classification.

cat_delivery.note: Both extractors tag on-time task completion/story points as Delivery, but these are task-completion (productivity) measures; no deployment, lead-time or cycle-time metric.

cat_agile.note: Story points for planning (Organization D) and daily meetings to track progress (Organization E); all organizations use Scrum/XP.

cat_survey.note: Semi-structured interviews on managers' perceptions; anonymous internal peer survey reported.

evidence.quote: This study employed a multi-method approach, combining qualitative and applied research.
The applied research section of this study used the Cross Industry Standard Process for Data Mining (CRISP-DM) framework
Twelve managers from six privately owned software houses in Indonesia, primarily those based in Batam, Medan, and Jakarta, were separately interviewed online from March 2024 to July 2024.

screenshots and accessed URLs from the work computers of developers in a cooperating software house were collected using recording programs to serve as primary data sources for the image and text datasets
machine learning models were developed to monitor developer activity by classifying screenshots captured during activity, along with the URL and text content scraped from accessed URLs.
by considering both effective working time and the total number of task story points completed.
All managers except p1 defined developer productivity as completing assigned tasks on time without compromising quality.
Based on their output, code quality, time taken to complete tasks
Organization E conducted monthly peer feedback meetings to gauge developers' impact on team dynamics beyond deliverables.
Organization A tracked real-time activity, Organization B used Git for code contribution tracking, and Organization C identified productivity based on story points.
Organization D used story points to help quantify productivity and aid in planning, prioritization, and goal alignment.
Organization E held daily meetings to track progress and resolve roadblocks to maintain developer productivity.
Semi-structured interviews were conducted to gain qualitative insights into software managers' perception of developer productivity
